country.comment: Primary empirical study conducted in Matungulu Sub-County, Machakos County, Kenya (other countries such as the United States, Ethiopia, the United Kingdom, and India are cited solely as background literature examples).
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title and Abstract; PDF p. 4, Materials and methods (The study area)

effect_estimate.comment: The inferential regression models Impact on Household Livelihoods as the dependent variable rather than direct water access, whereas household RHT financing, county integration responsibility, and incentive ratings are reported descriptively; note minor discrepancy between text (88%, PDF p. 6) and Figure 3 (87%, PDF p. 7) for head-of-household capital share.
effect_estimate.value: Integration of rainwater harvesting technologies (RHT) in the County Development Agenda was positively associated with Impact on Household Livelihoods in simple linear regression (unstandardized B = 0.611, SE = 0.027, standardized beta = 0.755, t = 22.351, p = 0.000; R^2 = 0.570, Adjusted R^2 = 0.569, F(1, 377) = 499.577, p = 0.000; N = 379; Pearson r = 0.755, p = 0.000), and water harvesting technologies correlated positively with household livelihoods (r = 0.703, p = 0.000, N = 379). Descriptively, only 0.3% of respondents attributed RWHT integration to county initiative (vs. 82% individual effort) and only 2% reported the county government as the main capital source to purchase/construct RHT (vs. 88% in text / 87% in Fig. 3 for head of household), although 95% (361/379) reported county empowerment programs and agreed county incentives encouraged RHT (composite mean = 4.04, SD = 0.699).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 5, Table 6; PDF pp. 6-10, Results (Figures 2-4, Tables 1-5)

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at <= 2 by cross-sectional design; rated 1 (documented association) because the study relies on cross-sectional respondent questionnaire scores, descriptive frequencies, and a bivariate linear association with household livelihoods rather than direct empirical observation of administrative or legal mechanisms operating on water access.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 5-10, Materials and methods (Data analysis) and Results (Tables 1-6, Figures 2-4)

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines county development planning and budgeting under MCIDP/CIDP and Water Act 2016 (planning), capital cost barriers and proposed county subsidies on water storage tanks and roofing materials (fees), county empowerment programs including farmer training, awareness creation, group funding, and tank provision (bureaucratic_assistance), and community/self-help group involvement in RHT integration (participation).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, planning, fees, bureaucratic_assistance, participation
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title and Abstract; PDF pp. 6-8, Results (Table 1, Figures 2-5); PDF pp. 10-11, Discussion and Conclusion

outcome_flags.comment: Examines household adoption and implementation of rainwater harvesting technologies to improve household water availability (water_access) and capital cost/affordability barriers to purchasing RHT systems and storage tanks (affordability).
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 6-8, Results (Figures 2-5); PDF p. 11, Discussion and Conclusion

publication_year.comment: Published 09/08/23 in East African Journal of Science, Technology and Innovation, Vol. 4 (Special Issue): August 2023.
publication_year.where_found: PDF p. 1, journal header, citation block, and publication history

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Observational quantitative cross-sectional household survey using descriptive statistics, correlation, and simple linear regression without a quasi-experimental intervention comparator or primary qualitative data collection.
risk_of_bias_tool.value: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

sample_size.comment: Sample calculated using Fisher's formula from a Sub-County population reported as 64,257 households (64,247 in Sampling procedure) with systematic probability sampling of farm households across two sub-locations; Tables 1, 2, and 3 report N = 379 respondents (Table 5 total df = 378).
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 4, Sampling procedure; PDF p. 7, Table 1; PDF p. 8, Table 2; PDF p. 9, Table 3; PDF p. 10, Table 5

study_design.comment: Primary quantitative data collected via structured questionnaires administered to systematically sampled farm households, complemented by secondary government and county planning documents (MCIDP 2015, CIDP 2018, Water Act 2016).
study_design.value: Cross-sectional household survey with descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, ANOVA, and simple linear regression, supplemented by secondary documentary review
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 4-6, Materials and methods
